# Gatekeeper

> ## Do not deploy this. It is a lab target.
>
> Gatekeeper contains **deliberate, documented defects at every tag**, including
> silent authorization and audit-integrity failures. An authorization service that
> lies in its own audit log looks perfectly healthy from the outside, which is the
> whole point of chapter 1 and exactly why it must never run anywhere real.
>
> Run it locally. Never on a public server, a shared network, or anything holding
> real data or real users. There is no supported production configuration.
> See [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md) and [defects.json](defects.json).
>
> **The gates are for lifting; the application is not.** The MIT license means
> take the pre-commit hook, the CI lanes, the analyzer config, the fitness tests
> and the branch-protection ruleset into your own projects. That is the
> deliverable. Gatekeeper is the patient.

> An access-control SaaS built in public, one quality gate at a time.

Gatekeeper is the running example and companion code for the book
**[AI: Programming Like a God: The Heavenly Gates](https://leanpub.com/ai-programming-like-a-god)**
by Tom Gilkison.

The book's premise: AI can write the code, but it cannot be trusted to
ship it. Gatekeeper starts life as an AI-generated app with no tests,
no CI, and no guardrails. Across the book it earns a layered system of
quality "gates" until its code is safe to merge on green, with the
human designing and verifying instead of typing.

## Follow along

Each chapter adds one gate. Every chapter's end state is a git tag, so
you can check out the code exactly as it stands at any point in the
book:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/TGilkison/Gatekeeper.git
cd Gatekeeper
git checkout chapter-06   # the code at the end of Chapter 6
```

## Tech

C# / .NET 8, ASP.NET Core Blazor Web App. Chosen for the strongest,
most cohesive quality-gate tooling of any mainstream stack: a real
compiler as the first gate, Roslyn analyzers, NetArchTest for
architecture, and Stryker.NET for mutation testing. The book explains
the why.

## License

MIT. Use it, fork it, copy the gate configs into your own projects.
That is the point: the book teaches you to build these gates; this repo
is where you can see them working and lift them.

## The book

[AI: Programming Like a God: The Heavenly Gates](https://leanpub.com/ai-programming-like-a-god)

  "defects": [

      "id": "V0-UNGATED",
      "severity": "informational",
      "provenance": "emergent",
      "title": "No gates of any kind",
      "detail": "No tests, no CI, no analyzers, no architecture rules, no rails. Nothing in the repository is capable of catching a defect. This is the state chapters 1 through 4 describe, and it is deliberate."
    },
    {
      "id": "V0-NO-DECISION-PATH",
      "severity": "informational",
      "provenance": "emergent",
      "title": "Stores policy, decides nothing",
      "detail": "Users, roles with a parent role, grants, an audit log and a Blazor console exist. Nothing answers whether a subject may take an action on a resource. The permission check is the harvest task, built from this tag."
    },
    {
      "id": "V0-MUTABLE-AUDIT",
      "severity": "high",
      "provenance": "emergent",
      "title": "Audit entries are freely mutable",
      "detail": "AuditLogEntry exposes public setters on every property and nothing prevents an update or a delete. An append-only audit log is the rule chapter 2 turns into a gate; at this tag the rule exists only in prose."
    },
    {
      "id": "V0-NO-CYCLE-DETECTION",
      "severity": "medium",
      "provenance": "emergent",
      "title": "Role graph has no cycle detection or depth cap",
      "detail": "A role may name a parent role with no check for a cycle and no bound on inheritance depth. Any future traversal of the role graph can loop forever."
    }
  ],

content.text:
The permission check is built and working end to end. Here's what I added.

## The decision engine

**`Services/AccessDecider.cs`** answers *can this subject do this action to this resource?* The resolution rules:

1. **Principals** = the subject itself, plus every role assigned to it, plus every ancestor role reached by walking `parent` links transitively.
2. **Matching grants** = grants hanging off any of those principals, for the same action, whose resource matches exactly (or is `*`).
3. **Precedence:** an explicit **Deny always beats an Allow**, and with no matching grant the answer is **Deny by default**.

The role walk has a visited-set cycle guard and a depth cap, so a malformed (cyclic) role graph can't loop forever.

## The HTTP surface (`Endpoints/DecisionApi.cs`, wired in `Program.cs`)

- **`POST /api/decisions`** → `{"effect":"Allow"|"Deny"}`. Every call writes one audit row recording *the effect actually returned*.
- **`GET /api/audit?subject=&resource=`** → decision entries, **oldest first**, in the exact `{subject, action, resource, outcome, timestamp}` shape with `…Z` UTC timestamps.
- **`PUT /api/policy`** → replaces the whole policy transactionally (roles, assignments, grants), validating effects up front so a bad grant can't leave it half-written.

## Data changes

New policy tables (`PolicyRole`, `PolicyAssignment`, `PolicyGrant`) plus three nullable decision columns on the existing `AuditLog`, all in migration `AddDecisionPolicyAndDecisionAudit`, applied on startup.

**Design note:** I kept the decision policy in its own tables rather than reusing the console's `Role`/`Grant` entities. The wire contract's subjects and role names are opaque strings with no tenant and no Identity user behind them, while `Grant`/`UserRole` carry required `CustomerId` and foreign keys into `AspNetUsers` — and "replaces the whole policy in one shot" describes a single self-contained store. Forcing the contract onto those entities would have meant fabricating Identity users to satisfy FKs. Decisions still land in the one shared audit log.

## Verified end to end (real HTTP against Postgres)

- The exact contract example (`user-42` / `document:delete` / `doc-7`) → `{"effect":"Deny"}` ✓
- Direct allow, and **inherited deny** through `Editor → Staff` ✓
- **Deny overrides Allow** when both match the same request ✓
- Audit **outcome equals the returned effect** (deny recorded as deny), oldest-first, correct field shape ✓
- Default-deny for unknown subjects, `*` wildcard resource, and `400`s for missing fields / invalid effect ✓

Build is clean (0 warnings, 0 errors). The app was left with the documented example policy loaded, and I stopped the background server.

Those last two verified behaviors are exactly the failure modes the repo's `defects.json` flags as arriving with this task — precedence collapse (H1a) and denied-recorded-as-allowed (H1b). This implementation gets both right; if the intent for the lab is to *seed* those defects rather than avoid them, say so and I'll introduce them deliberately.

## The decision engine

**`Services/AccessDecider.cs`** answers *can this subject do this action to this resource?* The resolution rules:

1. **Principals** = the subject itself, plus every role assigned to it, plus every ancestor role reached by walking `parent` links transitively.
2. **Matching grants** = grants hanging off any of those principals, for the same action, whose resource matches exactly (or is `*`).
3. **Precedence:** an explicit **Deny always beats an Allow**, and with no matching grant the answer is **Deny by default**.

The role walk has a visited-set cycle guard and a depth cap, so a malformed (cyclic) role graph can't loop forever.
